chapter: Hite tours, postwar L.A. and the Central Avenue scene
title: Poor Butterfly parody and Office of War Information broadcasts
summary: The Poor Butterfly parody, its later echo with the Treniers, and the Navy band recording weekly for the OWI.

blocks.x: So also in the -- back to this book, "it says, Hite In 1940, he said, "after leaving Height and working for several months with Cee Pee C.P. Johnson's band, Marshal joined forces with vibist violist Lionel Hampton."

Back to Cee Pee C.P. Johnson. I was thinking about your quote from "Poor Butterfly" that you mentioned as one of the numbers that was done with C.P. Johnson's band and you mentioned the lyric line, "That chick was high, like a big fat butterfly," and I remember hearing it some years later, in what? 1949, and the Treniers were using that line and probably that arrangement.
Well, the Treniers (PHONETIC) weren't even in existence at that time.
So what I wondered was if it lasted was that the that long, (Inaudible) beginning and that's what I wanted to ask (Inaudible) you about.

The beginning was out here in California. The Trenniers at that time were probably just starting into 'Bama State College, where they went and worked with the 'Bama State Collegians in Montgomery, Alabama. That's just around the time that they went in. So, they got into that somewhere way down the line because they didn't come into prominence until after World War II and we used that same melodic line for "Poor Butterfly" called "a big fat butterfly" for Office of War Information recordings that I made with the Navy Band, St. Mary's Preflight School, 1942, '43, '44, '45, and the only reason we were able to play "Poor Butterfly," which was a thing that is usually associated with Japanese, was that it was a parody and a put-on of the Japanese by the particular context of the words of "Poor Butterfly," like "That chick was high, like a big fat butterfly," you know. It was something that was not really eulogizing the Japanese, so we were able to use it in Office of War Information recordings during the time that I had the jazz band at St. Mary's Preflight School.
So, your band recorded (inaudible) there's probably . . . broadcasts (inaudible).
We recorded every week religiously, just like we had a regular job on the recording session, only we didn't get paid for it.
probably floating around right now, aren't they? (inaudible).

Yes, those recordings were made and put on all of our big battleships. They were played on the Office of War Information programs in the South Pacific mostly. As a matter of fact, after I was out of service, I used to get letters from Australia and from the various islands over in the South Pacific from people that had heard me on the Office of War Information programs, asking about the particular programs and wondering where the particular people were that were in the band and what we were doing, etcetera.
Before you made it a parody, did you add any Japanese references? The way to the lyrics?

Not at all. It was -- the take-off on the thing was actually about a woman. When we say "that chick was high," and by using the music of "Poor Butterfly," they just put "like a big fat butterfly," you know. Just a take-off. It was amusing.
